mcqs.question: A recursive function calls itself once on a problem of size n/3, then does O(n) non-recursive work. Which recurrence describes it?
mcqs.explanation: The recursive term reflects exactly what the call passes down — one call on n/3 — and the non-recursive work at this call is added on top, giving T(n) = T(n/3) + O(n). Reversing which number sits inside T(...) versus multiplying it, or shrinking by subtraction instead of division, describes a different function entirely.

mcqs.question: Using the recursion tree method on T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), why does the total work come out to O(n log n) rather than O(n²)?
options: Because merge sort's merge step is actually O(1), not O(n)
Because there are only 2 levels in the tree regardless of n
Because each of the log n levels contributes O(n) total work, and O(n) summed over log n levels is O(n log n)
Because the Master Theorem always rounds down to the smaller polynomial
mcqs.explanation: Doubling the node count each level exactly cancels the halved per-node work, so every level costs O(n) regardless of depth — and summing a constant O(n) across log n levels gives O(n log n), not a polynomial blow-up. It isn't a rounding convention; it falls straight out of counting levels and per-level cost.

mcqs.question: In the informal Master Theorem framing, what determines whether the recursive branching or the per-call work f(n) dominates the total complexity?
options: Whichever term was written first in the recurrence
The relative growth rates of n^(log_b a) (branching) versus f(n) (per-call work)
The total number of recursive calls made across the whole run
Whether the recursion uses one branch or two branches
mcqs.explanation: The Master Theorem compares how fast the branching factor grows the leaf count (n^(log_b a)) against how fast the non-recursive work f(n) grows — whichever grows faster asymptotically dominates the total. Branch count alone isn't sufficient; naive Fibonacci also branches twice per call but behaves nothing like merge sort.

mcqs.question: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) resolves to O(n log n), while T(n) = 2T(n-1) + O(1) resolves to O(2ⁿ). Both branch twice per call — what's the actual difference?
options: The second recurrence has more non-recursive work per call
The first recurrence only has one base case; the second has two
The first shrinks the input by a fraction each call (log n levels); the second shrinks by a fixed amount (n levels)
The second recurrence isn't actually recursive
mcqs.explanation: Shrinking by a fraction gives logarithmically many levels, so doubling the branch count each level is bounded by log n doublings — polynomial. Shrinking by a fixed amount gives n levels, so the same doubling compounds n times — exponential. The non-recursive work in both cases is O(1) or O(n) respectively and isn't what drives the exponential blow-up.

mcqs.question: Naive recursive Fibonacci calls itself twice per invocation, shrinking n by 1 each time. Roughly how does its call count grow from fib(30) to fib(40)?
options: It grows linearly, about 33% more calls
It grows by a small constant factor, similar to doubling the input in merge sort
It grows by roughly a thousand-fold, consistent with exponential (2ⁿ) growth
It stays about the same, since both fit comfortably on the call stack
mcqs.explanation: With T(n) = O(2ⁿ), going from n=30 to n=40 multiplies the call count by roughly 2¹⁰, about a thousand-fold — fib(30) makes millions of calls and fib(40) makes over a trillion. That explosive growth over just 10 more levels is the signature of exponential complexity, not a linear or mild increase.

mcqs.question: Merge sort makes roughly O(n) total recursive calls across its whole tree. Why is 'O(n) calls, so O(n) total time' the wrong conclusion?
options: Because the call count is actually O(n log n), not O(n)
Because recursive calls don't count toward total time at all
Because each call's non-recursive work isn't constant — it scales with the size of the slice that call received, which the tree-sum method accounts for and a raw call count does not
Because merge sort doesn't actually make O(n) calls
mcqs.explanation: Total work is calls multiplied by cost-per-call, and cost-per-call shrinks toward the leaves and is largest at the root — summing per-level work correctly captures that O(n log n) total, while counting only how many calls happened ignores that the calls aren't equally expensive.
